column9: Match each DNA base letter to the name of the base.
column16: C :: Cytosine
column28: A = adenine, T = thymine, C = cytosine, G = guanine. These four nitrogenous bases are the 'letters' of the DNA code.
column29: These are the four 'letters' of the DNA code.

column9: What does **DNA** stand for?
column16: Dinucleotide ribose acid
column28: DNA = deoxyribonucleic acid. 'Deoxyribo' comes from its sugar, deoxyribose, and 'nucleic acid' tells you what kind of molecule it is. The other choices mix up the word parts.
column29: Each part of the name tells you something about the molecule: one part comes from its sugar.

column9: Mia is cutting out paper pieces to model one of the small repeating units DNA is built from. Which three parts does she need? Select all that apply.
column16: A phosphate group
column28: Each repeating unit of DNA = phosphate group + 5-carbon sugar (deoxyribose) + nitrogenous base. Amino acids build proteins, glucose is a 6-carbon energy sugar, and hydrogen bonds join two units across the ladder; they are not part of one unit.
column29: Think about what DNA's full name tells you, and what makes up the sides and rungs of the ladder.

column9: In DNA, **adenine (A)** always pairs with which base?
column16: Cytosine (C)
column28: The base-pairing rule is A with T and C with G. Guanine pairs with cytosine, not adenine, and uracil is found only in RNA, not DNA.
column29: In DNA, there are only two kinds of pairs. Which one has A in it?

column9: In DNA, **guanine (G)** always pairs with ___.
column28: G always pairs with cytosine (C). The other pair is A with T.
column29: The two DNA pairs are A with T and G with ?.

column9: What is the shape of a DNA molecule?
column16: A double helix (two twisted strands)
column17: A flat ladder that does not twist
column28: DNA is two strands twisted around each other: a double helix, like a twisted ladder. A three-strand model was proposed in the 1950s, but it was wrong, and the ladder is twisted, not flat.
column29: Picture how many strands DNA has and whether they lie flat or wind around each other.

column9: In the twisted-ladder model of DNA, what makes up the **sides** of the ladder?
column15: Hydrogen bonds linked in a long chain
column16: Amino acids linked into a protein chain
column28: The sides (the backbone) are deoxyribose sugars and phosphate groups, one after the other. The base pairs are the rungs, hydrogen bonds hold each rung together in the middle, and amino acids are in proteins, not DNA.
column29: Two of the three parts of each building block line up end to end to make the long sides. Which two?

column9: In each building block of DNA, the nitrogenous base is attached to the sugar, not to the phosphate group.
column28: True. The base hangs off the deoxyribose sugar and points into the middle of the ladder. The phosphate links one sugar to the next sugar along the backbone.
column29: Picture one rail of the ladder: sugar, phosphate, sugar, phosphate. Which of those does each rung stick out from?

column9: Which sugar is part of every building block of DNA?
column16: Glucose
column28: DNA's sugar is deoxyribose, a 5-carbon sugar. Ribose is the sugar in RNA. Glucose and sucrose are energy sugars, not part of DNA's building blocks.
column29: DNA and RNA have slightly different sugars. Which one is named in DNA's full name?

column9: DNA is a long chain built from many small repeating units called ___.
column28: DNA is built from nucleotides. Each nucleotide has a phosphate group, a deoxyribose sugar, and a nitrogenous base.
column29: Each of these units has a phosphate group, a sugar, and a base.

column9: Why is DNA called the **molecule of heredity**?
column14: It stores energy for the cell, the way glucose does
column15: It carries the instructions for making proteins
column16: It forms the outer layer of the cell membrane
column17: It speeds up chemical reactions, the way enzymes do
column28: DNA controls traits by holding the instructions to make proteins, and proteins build and run the body. Copies of those instructions are passed from parents to offspring. Glucose stores energy, the membrane is mostly lipids, and enzymes (proteins) speed up reactions.
column29: Heredity means passing traits on. How does DNA control traits?

column9: A sample of frog DNA is **27% adenine**. What percent of the bases are **thymine**? Answer as a number (%).
column28: A pairs with T, so A = T. Adenine is 27%, so thymine is also 27%. (The other 46% is split evenly between G and C.)
column29: Which base does adenine pair with? Partners always come in equal amounts.

column9: Chargaff found that DNA always contains equal amounts of all four bases, 25% each.
column28: False. Chargaff found that A = T and G = C, but the four bases are not all equal. Human DNA, for example, is about 30% A, 30% T, 20% G, and 20% C.
column29: Think about which bases have to match each other. Do all four have to match?

column9: What type of macromolecule is DNA?
column16: A nucleic acid
column28: DNA (and RNA) are nucleic acids, the macromolecules that store and pass on genetic information. Proteins are made of amino acids, carbohydrates of sugars, and lipids of fatty acids.
column29: Think back to the four macromolecules from biochemistry. Which one stores genetic information?

column9: Where is the genetic code stored in a DNA molecule?
column14: In the number of its phosphate groups
column15: In the shape of its sugar molecules
column16: In the length of its hydrogen bonds
column17: In the order (sequence) of its bases
column28: The code is the order of the bases (A, T, C, G), like the order of letters in a sentence: change the order and you change the message. The number of phosphate groups, the shape of the sugars, and the hydrogen bonds do not carry the message; the hydrogen bonds just hold the two strands together.
column29: Think of DNA as a sentence. What makes one sentence say something different from another?

column9: Four students reported base percents for samples of double-stranded DNA. Which result **breaks** Chargaff's rule?
column28: Chargaff's rule says A = T and G = C. In 26/24/24/26, A (26%) does not equal T (24%) and G (24%) does not equal C (26%); it matches A with C, which is the wrong pairing. The other three samples have A = T and G = C. The bases do not have to be 25% each, so 15/15/35/35 is fine.
column29: For each sample, compare adenine with its partner and guanine with its partner.

column9: DNA from a corn plant is **22% cytosine**. What percent of the bases are **adenine**? Answer as a number (%).
column28: C = G, so G = 22% and C + G = 44%. That leaves 100 − 44 = 56% for A + T. A = T, so A = 56 ÷ 2 = 28%.
column29: Find G first. Subtract C + G from 100%, then split what is left between A and T.

column9: A sample of salmon DNA is **29% thymine**. What percent of the bases are **guanine**? Answer as a number (%).
column28: T = A, so A = 29% and A + T = 58%. That leaves 100 − 58 = 42% for G + C. G = C, so G = 42 ÷ 2 = 21%.
column29: Find A first. Subtract A + T from 100%, then split what is left between G and C.

column9: Which pair lists two **purines**?
column16: Adenine and thymine
column28: Purines are the double-ring bases, adenine (A) and guanine (G). Thymine and cytosine are single-ring pyrimidines. A–T and G–C are base pairs, and every base pair has one purine and one pyrimidine, so neither pair can be two purines.
column29: Purines have a double ring. Two bases that pair with each other can't both be purines.

column9: In DNA, a purine always pairs with a pyrimidine. Why is that important?
column14: Two pyrimidines would form stronger bonds than any other pair
column15: Purines can only bond to sugars, never to other bases
column16: A double-ring plus a single-ring base keeps every rung the same width
column17: Pyrimidines are found on only one of the two strands
column28: A purine (double ring) + a pyrimidine (single ring) makes every rung the same width, so the sides of the ladder stay evenly spaced. Two purines would be too wide and two pyrimidines too narrow. Both kinds of bases are on both strands and bond to each other in the middle.
column29: Think about size. What would happen to the ladder if two big bases, or two small bases, were paired?

column9: How many hydrogen bonds hold a **G–C** base pair together?
column28: A G–C pair is held by 3 hydrogen bonds, and an A–T pair by 2. That is why G–C pairs hold together a little more tightly.
column29: The A–T pair and the G–C pair don't use the same number of hydrogen bonds. Which pair holds on more tightly?

column9: Every organism has the same order of bases in its DNA; organisms differ only in how much DNA they have.
column28: False. The order of the bases is different in different organisms. A different order means different instructions, so different proteins and traits.
column29: If the code is the order of the bases, what would happen if every organism had the same order?

column9: What do the labels **5'** and **3'** (five-prime and three-prime) on a DNA strand refer to?
column14: The numbered bases at each end
column15: The numbered hydrogen bonds at each end
column16: The numbered phosphate groups at each end
column17: The numbered sugar carbons at each end
column28: The carbons in deoxyribose are numbered 1' to 5'. One end of a strand ends at a sugar's 5' carbon (where the phosphate attaches), and the other ends at a 3' carbon. That is how you tell which way a strand runs. The labels do not number bases, phosphate groups, or hydrogen bonds.
column29: The prime numbers come from numbering atoms in one part of the nucleotide.

column9: Which of these strand-and-partner pairs follow the DNA base-pairing rules? Select all that apply.
column16: CCGA paired with GGCT
column28: Check each base: A–T and C–G. AGTC → TCAG, CCGA → GGCT, and ATTG → TAAC all follow the rules. CGCG should pair with GCGC (its 3rd base, C, needs a G, not a T), TTAC with AATG (its 1st base, T, needs an A, not a C), and GATC with CTAG (its 2nd base, A, needs a T, not a G).
column29: Go letter by letter. Every A needs a T, every T needs an A, every C needs a G, and every G needs a C. One wrong letter breaks the pair.

column9: One strand of a DNA segment reads **A T G C C A**. What is the base sequence of the strand paired with it?
column14: T A C G G T
column15: A T G C C A
column16: U A C G G U
column17: G C A T T G
column28: Pair each base: A→T, T→A, G→C, C→G, C→G, A→T, which gives TACGGT. Copying the same letters is not pairing, U is only found in RNA, and GCATTG swaps in the wrong partners (A with G, T with C).
column29: Go one base at a time using A–T and C–G.

column9: Before the 1950s, many scientists thought **proteins**, not DNA, carried hereditary information. Why?
column14: Proteins are found only in the nucleus, but DNA is not
column15: Proteins use 20 kinds of amino acids; DNA has only 4 bases
column16: DNA was not discovered until the 1950s, when its shape was found
column17: Proteins can make copies of themselves, but DNA cannot
column28: Proteins seemed more complex: long chains built from 20 different amino acids, compared to only 4 bases in DNA. Scientists expected the more complex molecule to hold the information. DNA was discovered in 1869, long before its shape was worked out; proteins are found all through the cell (not only in the nucleus), while DNA is kept in the nucleus; and DNA is the molecule that gets copied.
column29: Scientists expected the hereditary molecule to be the more complicated one. Which is built from more kinds of building blocks?

column9: Match each scientist to their part in the story of DNA's structure.
column14: Erwin Chargaff :: Measured the amounts of the four bases in many organisms
column15: Rosalind Franklin :: Took X-ray diffraction photos showing that DNA is a helix
column16: Watson and Crick :: Built the first accurate model of DNA in 1953
column17: Maurice Wilkins :: Shared the 1962 Nobel Prize with Watson and Crick
column28: Chargaff measured the bases (and found A = T, G = C). Franklin's X-ray diffraction photos showed that DNA is a helix. Watson and Crick used her X-ray images to build the first correct model in 1953. Wilkins, who worked with Franklin's X-ray data, shared the 1962 Nobel Prize with them (Franklin had died in 1958).
column29: Think about who measured, who photographed, who built the model, and who shared a prize with the builders.

column9: One strand of DNA runs 5' to 3' and the other runs 3' to 5'. Because the strands run in opposite directions, they are called ___.
column28: The strands are antiparallel: side by side (parallel) but pointing in opposite (anti) directions, like the two lanes of a two-way road.
column29: Think of the two lanes of a two-way road: side by side, but heading in opposite directions. DNA's strands have a special name for this.

column9: Which part of a DNA nucleotide is different from one nucleotide to the next?
column16: Both the sugar and the phosphate
column28: Every DNA nucleotide has the same phosphate and the same deoxyribose sugar; only the base changes (A, T, C, or G).
column29: There are only four kinds of DNA nucleotides. What makes them different from each other?

column9: Ty's DNA model is a double helix with **40 base pairs**. How many nucleotides are in his model?
column28: Each base pair is two nucleotides, one on each strand. 40 base pairs × 2 = 80 nucleotides.
column29: One rung of the ladder has a base from each side. How many nucleotides is that per rung?

column9: Human DNA and bacteria DNA use the same four bases and follow the same base-pairing rules.
column28: True. All living things use A, T, C, and G with the same pairing rules (A–T, C–G). The rules come from the bases themselves, so they work the same way in every organism.
column29: Does the pairing rule depend on the organism, or is it built into the bases themselves?

column9: A single strand of DNA has **12 nucleotides**. How many phosphate groups does it have?
column28: Every nucleotide has exactly one phosphate group, one sugar, and one base. 12 nucleotides → 12 phosphate groups. 36 would be counting all three parts, and 24 would be counting two strands.
column29: How many phosphate groups are in one nucleotide?

column9: When the two strands of DNA are pulled apart (unzipped), which bonds are broken?
column14: The bonds between each sugar and its phosphate
column15: The bonds between each base and its sugar
column16: The bonds between the phosphate groups
column17: The hydrogen bonds between the paired bases
column28: Unzipping breaks the weak hydrogen bonds in the middle of each rung. The strong covalent bonds in the backbone, and between each base and its sugar, stay together, so each strand stays in one piece.
column29: Unzipping splits every rung down the middle. What holds the two halves of a rung together?

column9: A DNA sample is **34% adenine**. What percent is **cytosine**?
column28: A = T = 34%, so A + T = 68%. G + C = 100 − 68 = 32%, and C = 32 ÷ 2 = 16%. 32% is G and C together (you still have to split it in half), 34% is thymine, and 66% is 100 − 34, which forgets that thymine is also 34%.
column29: Find A + T first. Whatever is left over is shared equally by G and C.

column9: Ella says a DNA molecule is like a **spiral staircase**. Which part of the staircase matches the **base pairs**?
column16: The steps
column28: The base pairs run across the middle like the steps. The two handrails match the sugar-phosphate backbones that spiral around the outside.
column29: Base pairs connect one side to the other across the middle. Which part of a staircase does that?

column9: A DNA sample is **18% guanine**. What percent of the bases are **thymine**? Answer as a number (%).
column29: Find G + C first, subtract from 100%, then split what is left between A and T.

column9: A short double-stranded DNA molecule has **1,000 bases** in all. **340** of them are adenine. How many are **cytosine**?
column29: Chargaff's rule works for numbers of bases, not just percents. Find T first.

column9: A short DNA segment has **6 A–T pairs** and **4 G–C pairs**. How many hydrogen bonds hold the two strands together?
column28: A–T pairs have 2 hydrogen bonds and G–C pairs have 3. (6 × 2) + (4 × 3) = 12 + 12 = 24 hydrogen bonds.
column29: Multiply each kind of pair by its number of hydrogen bonds, then add.

column9: Two DNA samples are the same length. Sample X is **60% G + C**. Sample Y is **30% G + C**. Which sample needs more heat to separate its strands?
column14: Sample Y, because A–T pairs have more hydrogen bonds
column15: Sample X, because G–C pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds
column16: Neither; the same length means the same bonds
column17: Sample Y, because A–T pairs are both purines
column28: G–C pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds and A–T pairs have 2. Sample X has more G–C pairs, so it has more hydrogen bonds to break and needs more heat. Same length does not mean the same number of bonds, and A–T is a purine–pyrimidine pair, not two purines.
column29: Count bonds, not bases. Which kind of pair holds on with more hydrogen bonds?

column9: Lena says, "If a DNA sample is 20% adenine, then it must also be 20% guanine." Is she right?
column14: Yes. All four bases are always equal
column15: No. G pairs with A, so G is 80%
column16: No. A and T are 40% together, so G is 30%
column17: No. G + C must equal A, so G is 10%
column28: A = T = 20%, so A + T = 40%. That leaves 60% for G + C, so G = 30%. The bases are not always equal, and G pairs with C, not A.
column29: Adenine's partner is thymine, not guanine. Use A and T to find out how much is left for G and C.

column9: A lab measured the bases in six DNA samples. Which results could come from normal double-stranded DNA? Select all that apply.
column28: Real double-stranded DNA needs A = T, G = C, and a total of 100%. 12/12/38/38, 31/31/19/19, and 25/25/25/25 pass. 30/20/30/20 has A ≠ T, 40/40/15/15 adds up to 110%, and 35/35/20/10 has G ≠ C.
column29: Check two things for each sample: do the partners match, and do the four numbers add up to 100%?

column9: How does base pairing make it possible for DNA to be copied?
column14: The two strands are identical, so copying just repeats one strand
column15: The sugar-phosphate backbone stores a backup copy of the bases
column16: Hydrogen bonds are strong enough to hold both strands while copying
column17: Each strand's bases set its partner's bases, so either strand is a pattern
column28: Because A only pairs with T and C only with G, one strand tells you exactly what the other strand must be. Split the strands, and each one can be used as a pattern to build a new partner. The strands are complementary, not identical, the backbone doesn't store bases, and the hydrogen bonds are weak so the strands can separate.
column29: If you know one strand, can you figure out the other one? How would that help a cell make a copy?

column9: Put these in order so that each item is a part of the next one, starting with the **smallest** part.
column16: Chromosome
column28: A base is one part of a nucleotide. Many nucleotides make a gene (a section of DNA). Many genes are found along one DNA molecule, and a chromosome is a DNA molecule coiled up with proteins.
column29: Start with one piece of a nucleotide. What is that piece a part of?

column9: A DNA segment has **50 base pairs**. **20** of them are A–T pairs, and the rest are G–C pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold this segment together?
column28: G–C pairs = 50 − 20 = 30. A–T: 20 × 2 = 40. G–C: 30 × 3 = 90. Total = 40 + 90 = 130 hydrogen bonds.
column29: First find how many G–C pairs there are. Then count bonds for each kind of pair and add.

column9: Data table (% of each base): Human: A 30.3, T 30.3, G 19.5, C 19.5 | Wheat: A 27.3, T 27.1, G 22.7, C 22.8 | E. coli: A 24.7, T 23.6, G 26.0, C 25.7. Which conclusion does the data support?
column14: A is close to T and G is close to C, but amounts differ by species
column15: All four bases are close to 25% in every organism in the table
column16: A is close to G and T is close to C in every organism in the table
column17: Humans have more total DNA than wheat or E. coli bacteria have
column28: In every row, A is about the same as T and G is about the same as C (small differences are measurement error), but the percents change from species to species. The bases are not all close to 25% (human DNA is about 30% A), A does not match G, and percents tell you nothing about the total amount of DNA.
column29: Compare A to T and G to C within each row, then compare the rows to each other.

column9: In any double-stranded DNA molecule, purines (A + G) make up exactly half of the bases.
column28: True. Every base pair has one purine (A or G) and one pyrimidine (T or C). So purines are always half the bases, no matter the organism. (A + G = T + C.)
column29: How many purines are in each base pair?

column9: In a DNA sample, A and T together make up **62%** of the bases. What percent of the bases are **cytosine**? Answer as a number (%).
column29: Whatever is not A or T must be G or C, and G and C come in equal amounts.

column9: Sam says, "Along one strand, the bases must follow a rule, like A always next to T." Rosa says, "Only bases across from each other follow a rule; the order along a strand can be anything." Who is right?
column14: Sam; A must always sit next to T on the same strand
column15: Rosa; pairing rules only apply across the two strands
column16: Both; the bases follow rules in both directions
column17: Neither; bases can pair with any base across
column28: The pairing rules (A–T, C–G) are for the bases across from each other. Along one strand, the bases can come in any order, and that order is the genetic code. If the order were fixed, DNA couldn't hold different instructions.
column29: If the order along a strand were fixed, could DNA hold different instructions for different genes?

column9: A virus's DNA is **A 32%, T 18%, G 24%, C 26%**. What is the best explanation?
column14: Its DNA is double-stranded but has some extra adenine
column15: Chargaff's rule only works for the DNA of plants and animals
column16: Its DNA is single-stranded, so its bases are not paired
column17: The sample must have contained uracil instead of thymine
column28: A = T and G = C only works when bases are paired across two strands. Here A ≠ T and G ≠ C, so this DNA can't be double-stranded; some viruses have single-stranded DNA. Double-stranded DNA can't have extra adenine, because every A needs a T partner. Chargaff's rule works for all double-stranded DNA, not just plants and animals, and uracil is found in RNA, not DNA.
column29: Chargaff's rule comes from bases being paired. What if there's nothing to pair with?

column9: One strand of DNA is **5'-GGATCA-3'**. Which answer correctly shows its partner strand, with the ends labeled?
column16: 3'-CCUAGU-5'
column28: Pair each base (G→C, G→C, A→T, T→A, C→G, A→T) to get CCTAGT, and because the strands are antiparallel, the partner runs 3' to 5' under the 5' to 3' strand. 5'-CCTAGT-3' has the right bases but the wrong direction, 3'-GGATCA-5' copies the strand instead of pairing it, and U is only in RNA.
column29: Get the bases with A–T and C–G, then remember the two strands point in opposite directions.
